General Comments
The authors depict a Bayesian model and inference algorithm for deconvolutions of potentially noisy
and partially observed images. The emphasis is on computation and the authors are exceptionally
detailed in the mathematics and practicalities of the algorithm: a reader could quite reasonably
implement the method using this manuscript.
However, the innovations over Senn et al. (2025) are not clear. From the Introduction of
the manuscript: “ Our contribution is threefold. First, we formulate the model outside its original
seismic setting. Second, we derive an explicit eigenvalue-based representation of the posterior com-
putations and Gibbs sampler, so that the main updates can be implemented directly in the spectral
domain. Third, we introduce a marginal blur update obtained by analytically integrating out the
image from the joint blur-image conditional and sampling the resulting marginal blur conditional
with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC). ”
Substantial movement on this first point is critical, since JCGS is not a geophysical journal.
The method needs to be formulated and applicable outside of the original seismic application.
But the assumptions of 1) a vertical/horizontal separable prior, 2) row-uniform observations, and
3) a 1-dimensional convolution kernel would be prohibitive for any other canonical deconvolution
application (Gaussian, defocus, motion blur, such as in the seminal papers cited in the current
manuscript, Levin et al., (2009); Babacan et al., (2012); Orieux et al., (2010); Park et al., (2012)).
These assumptions are buried within the middle of the manuscript (except for the 1D kernel, which
is in the abstract) and are in conflict with the title, “ Bayesian Semi-Blind Deconvolution at Scale ”
and the general 2D deconvolution statement in equation 1, which suggest a very general method
to a researcher searching the literature. The method is only tested on simulated 1D images (for
which all the above restrictions are vaccuous) and a seismic dataset with a single well observation.
For a statistics journal, the paper would be much improved by relaxing the above restrictions and
demonstrating applicability in another domain.
On the second and third contributions, the benefit of Gibbs updates in the spectral domain over
Senn et al. (2025) is never explicitly stated, and the collapsed HMC update provides improvements
in limited scenarios, by the authors’ admission. But the weight of any improvements on these fronts
is entirely conditional of the applicability of the method.
Specific Comments
1. Reading the paper in sequence, I found Section 2.1 confusing and over-engineered, primarily
because the reasons behind the formulation (which are good reasons!) are not apparent until
much later in the manuscript.
The authors introduce the general linear Gaussian model y =Ax +e and the conditional
distribution forx|y. But later the authors supposee = 0,A is a selector matrix (soAx =xc),
and Ax = b (so xc = b). At first read, this raises the question “Why not just sample
xu|(xc = b)?”. Quantities A and e seem like dead weight, and the dismissed alternative,
forming the singular N(µ∗, Σ∗) and sampling, is a straw man, since the obvious competitor
is the non-singular conditional for xu.
Algorithm 1 is attractive, but not for the reasons given in Section 2.1: the unconstrained
covariance is circulant (Sections 3 & 4), so Step 1 of Algorithm 1 is cheap, while subset-
ting destroys that structure with little reduction in dimension if k≪ n. The reason given,
that conditioning by Kriging “can be computationally efficient for k < n ”, is not true for a
generic matrix, where conditioning by Kriging is actually strictly worse than the partitioned
1
conditional.
Further, the authors handle two different cases, one where A is a selector and e = 0 and
another where A is general and e∼ N(0, Σe). So the general equation is truly warranted,
but this is not clear in Section 2.1.
I encourage the authors to clearly delineate the two cases they will deal with and forecast
why Algorithm 1 will be preferable to the more obvious xu|(xc =b) sampler.
2. Page 7, Line 31 : Should be “Hermitian transpose”, or conjugate transpose, which is more
common.
3. Equations 5 and 9, the conjugate transpose should be on the right F n. Further, the eigen-
values just below Equation 9 are missing a √mn factor.
4. Page 8, Line 4 and 17 : “eigenvalue-based operations”? I do not think that is a standard
term. The listed operations end up only affecting the eigenvalues (because of the shared
eigenvectors), but that’s a consequence, not a definition for that set of operations.
5. Section 2.3 : Would the authors please justify their choice of a horizontal-vertical separability?
In general, this is a limiting choice for a generic spatial field, and is not required for a circulant
embedding (Wood and Chan, 1994, Dietrich and Newsam, 1997). It may be appropriate for
the intended geophysical application, however. Also, the order Σh⊗Σv, assumes thex lattice
is vectorized column-major, which probably should be stated explicitly in the manuscript.
6. Page 11, Line 1: “ We assume that the additional image information consists in m exactly
observed pixels at the same rows of a subset of columns in the image ”. It would be best to write
this out explicitly and mathematically. But more importantly, this is highly restrictive, and
buried in the middle of the paper. Again, perhaps this restriction is fine for the geophysical
application (wells within an area tend to be drilled to a standardized depth?), but it would
be prohibitive elsewhere.
7. Page 11, Paragraph 2: Again, a 1D stationary blur kernel is very restrictive...
